implementation_notes: Kotlin/JVM reuses the JDK structure: ConcurrentLinkedQueue - documented as an efficient non-blocking algorithm - is used straight from Kotlin and is the default for shared hand-off in JVM code. For coroutine-shaped code the idiomatic replacement is kotlinx.coroutines Channel<T>: send/receive suspend instead of spinning, fan-out and fan-in are built in, and a buffered channel expresses backpressure without atomics - use it unless the producer must be non-suspending, in which case trySend() or the JDK queue fits. Kotlin has no lock-free queue of its own, so multiplatform targets (Native/JS) cannot use the JDK classes and need an expect/actual split or a third-party structure.
pitfalls: poll() in a loop is a spin on the JVM; coroutine consumers should use Channel.receive or a BlockingQueue to park instead.
A Channel is not the JDK queue: consumers must be coroutines, and an unbounded channel has the same unbounded-growth failure mode as an unbounded queue.
Multiplatform targets have no java.util.concurrent - keep the queue behind an expect/actual interface so the JVM type does not leak into shared sources.
